Mercury had told the band he "wasn't feeling that great" and stated, "I will finish it when I come back next time". He
never made it back into the studio, so May later recorded the final verse of the song.
Tributes
A statue in Montreux, Switzerland, by sculptor Irena Sedlecká, was erected as a tribute to Mercury. It stands almost 10
ft high overlooking Lake Geneva and was unveiled on 25 November 1996 by Mercury's father and Montserrat Caballé,
with bandmates Brian May and Roger Taylor also in attendance. Beginning in 2003 fans from around the world have
gathered in Switzerland annually to pay tribute to the singer as part of the "Freddie Mercury Montreux Memorial Day"
on the first weekend of September.
In 1997 the three remaining members of Queen released "No-One but You (Only the Good Die Young)", a song
dedicated to Mercury and all those that die too soon. In 1999 a Royal Mail stamp with an image of Mercury on stage
was issued in his honour as part of the UK postal service's Millennium Stamp series. In 2009 a star commemorating
Mercury was unveiled in Feltham, west London where his family moved upon arriving in England in 1964. The star in
memory of Mercury's achievements was unveiled on Feltham High Street by his mother Jer Bulsara and Queen
bandmate May.
A statue of Mercury stood over the entrance to the Dominion Theatre in London's <color=#3366CC>West End</color> from May 2002 to May
2014 for Queen and Ben Elton's musical We Will Rock You. A tribute to Queen was on display at the Fremont Street
Experience in downtown Las Vegas throughout 2009 on its video canopy. In December 2009 a large model of Mercury
wearing tartan was displayed in Edinburgh as publicity for the run of We Will Rock You. Sculptures of Mercury often
feature him wearing a military jacket with his fist in the air. In 2018, <color=#3366CC>GQ</color> called Mercury's yellow military jacket (created
by British costume designer Diana Moseley) from his 1986 concerts his best known look, while <color=#3366CC>CNN</color> called it "an iconic
moment in fashion."
For Mercury's 65th birthday in 2011, Google dedicated its Google Doodle to him. It included an animation set to his
song, "Don't Stop Me Now". Referring to "the late, great Freddie Mercury" in their 2012 <color=#3366CC>Rock and Roll Hall of Fame</color>
induction speech, <color=#3366CC>Guns N' Roses</color> quoted Mercury's lyrics from "We Are the Champions"; "I've taken my bows, my
curtain calls, you've brought me fame and fortune and everything that goes with it, and I thank you all."
Tribute was paid to Queen and Mercury at the closing ceremony of the 2012 Summer Olympics in London. The band's
performance of "We Will Rock You" with Jessie J was opened with a video of Mercury's "call and response" routine
from 1986's Wembley Stadium performance, with the 2012 crowd at the Olympic Stadium responding appropriately.
The frog genus Mercurana, discovered in 2013 in <color=#3366CC>Kerala</color>, India, was named as a tribute because Mercury's "vibrant
music inspires the authors". The site of the discovery is very near to where Mercury spent most of his childhood. In
2013, a newly discovered species of <color=#3366CC>damselfly</color> from Brazil was named Heteragrion freddiemercuryi, honouring the
"superb and gifted musician and songwriter whose wonderful voice and talent still entertain millions" — one of four
similar damselflies named after the Queen bandmates, in tribute to Queen's 40th anniversary.
On 1 September 2016, an English Heritage blue plaque was unveiled at Mercury's home in 22 Gladstone Avenue in
Feltham, west London by his sister, Kashmira Cooke, and Brian May. Attending the ceremony, Karen Bradley, the UK
Secretary of State for Culture, called Mercury "one of Britain's most influential musicians", and added he "is a global
icon whose music touched the lives of millions of people around the world". On 24 February 2020 a street in Feltham
was renamed Freddie Mercury Close during a ceremony attended by his sister Kashmira. On 5 September 2016, the
70th anniversary of Mercury's birth, asteroid 17473 Freddiemercury was named after him. Issuing the certificate of
designation to the "charismatic singer", Joel Parker of the Southwest Research Institute added: "Freddie Mercury sang,
'I'm a shooting star leaping through the sky' — and now that is even more true than ever before." In an April 2019
interview, British rock concert promoter Harvey Goldsmith referred to Mercury as "one of our most treasured talents".
In August 2019, Mercury was one of the honorees inducted in the Rainbow Honor Walk, a walk of fame in San
Francisco's Castro District noting <color=#3366CC>LGBTQ</color> people who have "made significant contributions in their fields". Freddie
Mercury Alley is a 107 yd alley next to the British embassy in the Ujazdów district in <color=#3366CC>Warsaw</color>, Poland, which is
dedicated to Mercury, and was unveiled on 22 November 2019. Until the Freddie Mercury Close in Feltham was
dedicated, Warsaw was the only city in Europe with a street dedicated to the singer. In January 2020, Queen became
the first band to join Queen Elizabeth II on a British coin. Issued by the Royal Mint, the commemorative £5 coin
features the instruments of all four band members, including Mercury's Bechstein grand piano and his mic and stand. In
April 2022, a life-size statue of Mercury was unveiled in South Korea's resort island of <color=#3366CC>Jeju</color>. In May 2024, the crater
Bulsara on the planet <color=#3366CC>Mercury</color> was named after his birth name.
Mercury has featured in international advertising to represent the UK. In 2001, a parody of Mercury, along with prints of
other British music icons consisting of <color=#3366CC>the Beatles</color>, Elton John, <color=#3366CC>Spice Girls</color>, and <color=#3366CC>the Rolling Stones</color>, appeared in the
<color=#3366CC>Eurostar</color> national advertising campaign in France for the Paris to London route. In September 2017 the airline
Norwegian painted the tail fin of two of its aircraft with a portrait of Mercury to mark what would have been his 71st
birthday. Mercury is one of the company's six "British tail fin heroes", alongside England's 1966 FIFA World Cup

winning captain <color=#3366CC>Bobby Moore</color>, children's author <color=#3366CC>Roald Dahl</color>, novelist <color=#3366CC>Jane Austen</color>, pioneering pilot <color=#3366CC>Amy Johnson</color>, and
aviation entrepreneur Sir Freddie Laker.
Since 2021, one of the houses where Mercury lived in Stone Town has hosted a Freddie Mercury Museum, which
features many photographs and dozens of handwritten song lyrics. The museum is studiously silent on many matters
that would be culturally or politically sensitive in Zanzibar, including Mercury's sexual preferences, his death of AIDS
complications, and the fact that it was the slaughter of Arabs and Indians that forced his family to leave in 1964.
Importance in AIDS history
As the first major rock star to die of AIDS-related complications, Mercury's death represented an important event in the
history of the disease. In April 1992, the remaining members of Queen founded The Mercury Phoenix Trust and
organised The Freddie Mercury Tribute Concert for AIDS Awareness, to celebrate the life and legacy of Mercury and
raise money for AIDS research, which took place on 20 April 1992. The Mercury Phoenix Trust has since raised
millions of pounds for various AIDS charities. The tribute concert, which took place at London's Wembley Stadium for
an audience of 72,000, featured a wide variety of guests including <color=#3366CC>Robert Plant</color> (of <color=#3366CC>Led Zeppelin</color>), Roger Daltrey (of <color=#3366CC>the</color>

<color=#3366CC>Who</color>), Extreme, <color=#3366CC>Elton John</color>, <color=#3366CC>Metallica</color>, <color=#3366CC>David Bowie</color>, Annie Lennox, Tony Iommi (of <color=#3366CC>Black Sabbath</color>), <color=#3366CC>Guns N' Roses</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Elizabeth Taylor</color>, <color=#3366CC>George Michael</color>, <color=#3366CC>Def Leppard</color>, Seal and <color=#3366CC>Liza Minnelli</color>, with <color=#3366CC>U2</color> also appearing via satellite. Elizabeth
Taylor spoke of Mercury as "an extraordinary rock star who rushed across our cultural landscape like a comet shooting
across the sky". The concert was broadcast live to 76 countries and had an estimated viewing audience of 1 billion
people. The Freddie for a Day fundraiser on behalf of the Mercury Phoenix Trust takes place every year in London, with
supporters of the charity including <color=#3366CC>Monty Python</color> comedian <color=#3366CC>Eric Idle</color> and Mel B of the Spice Girls.
The documentary Freddie Mercury - The Final Act aired on BBC Two in 2021 and <color=#3366CC>The CW</color> in the US in April 2022. It
covered Mercury's last days, how his bandmates and friends put together the tribute concert at Wembley, and
interviewed medical professionals, people who tested HIV positive, and others who knew someone who died of AIDS.
At the 50th International Emmy Awards in 2022, it won the International Emmy Award for Best Arts Programming.
Appearances in lists of influential individuals
Several popularity polls conducted over the past decade indicate that Mercury's reputation may have been enhanced
since his death. For instance, in a 2002 vote to determine who the UK public considers the greatest British people in
history, Mercury was ranked 58 in the list of the 100 Greatest Britons, broadcast by the BBC. He was further listed at
the 52nd spot in a 2007 Japanese national survey of the 100 most influential heroes. Although he had been criticised
by gay activists for hiding his HIV status, author Paul Russell included Mercury in his book The Gay 100: A Ranking of
the Most Influential Gay Men and Lesbians, Past and Present. In 2008, <color=#3366CC>Rolling Stone</color> ranked Mercury 18 on its Top 100
Singers Of All Time. Mercury was voted the greatest male singer in <color=#3366CC>MTV</color>'s 22 Greatest Voices in Music. In 2011 a
Rolling Stone readers' pick placed Mercury in second place of the magazine's Best Lead Singers of All Time. <color=#3366CC>Billboard</color>
magazine placed him second on their 25 Best Rock Frontmen (and Women) of All Time list in 2015, and third on their
50 Greatest Rock Lead Singers of All Time list in 2023. In 2016, LA Weekly ranked him first on the list of 20 greatest
singers of all time, in any genre. In 2023, Rolling Stone ranked Mercury at No. 14 on its list of the 200 Greatest Singers
of All Time. In 2026, Consequence ranked Mercury the best vocalist of all time.
Portrayal on stage
On 24 November 1997, a <color=#3366CC>monodrama</color> about Freddie Mercury's life, titled Mercury: The Afterlife and Times of a Rock
God, opened in New York City. It presented Mercury in the hereafter: examining his life, seeking redemption and
searching for his true self. The play was written and directed by Charles Messina and the part of Mercury was played
by Khalid Gonçalves (né Paul Gonçalves) and then later, Amir Darvish. Billy Squier opened one of the shows with an
acoustic performance of a song he had written about Mercury titled "I Have Watched You Fly".
In 2016 a musical titled Royal Vauxhall premiered at the Royal Vauxhall Tavern in Vauxhall, London. Written by
Desmond O'Connor, the musical told the alleged tales of the nights that Mercury, Kenny Everett and <color=#3366CC>Diana, Princess of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Wales</color> spent out at the Royal Vauxhall Tavern in London in the 1980s. Following several successful runs in London, the
musical was taken to the Edinburgh Fringe Festival in August 2016 starring Tom Giles as Mercury.
Portrayal in film and television
The 2018 biographical film Bohemian Rhapsody was, at its release, the highest-grossing <color=#3366CC>musical</color> biographical film of all
time. Mercury was portrayed by Rami Malek, whose performance earned him the Academy Award, BAFTA Award,
Golden Globe Award and Screen Actors Guild Award for Best Actor. While the film received mixed reviews and
contained historical inaccuracies, it won the Golden Globe for Best Motion Picture – Drama.
Mercury appeared as a supporting character in the BBC television drama Best Possible Taste: The Kenny Everett
Story, first broadcast in October 2012. He was portrayed by actor James Floyd. He was played by actor John Blunt in
The Freddie Mercury Story: Who Wants to Live Forever, first broadcast in the UK on Channel 5 in November 2016.
Although the programme was criticised for focusing on Mercury's love life and sexuality, Blunt's performance and
likeness to the singer did receive praise.
In 2018, David Avery portrayed Mercury in the Urban Myths comedy series in an episode focusing on the antics
backstage at Live Aid, and Kayvan Novak portrayed Mercury in an episode titled "<color=#3366CC>The Sex Pistols</color> vs. Bill Grundy". He
was also portrayed by Eric McCormack (as the character Will Truman) on Will & Grace in the October 2018 episode
titled "Tex and the City".
Auction
From 4 August to 5 September 2023, an exhibition titled, Freddie Mercury: A World of His Own, saw almost 1,500 items
of Mercury's, which he had given to his former partner Mary Austin, displayed at Sotheby's in New Bond Street, London
before being sold across six auctions. Nearly 140,000 fans visited the exhibition, which Sotheby's had called "the life
and work of Britain's greatest rock showman of the 20th century".
A <color=#3366CC>Yamaha</color> baby grand piano used by Mercury to compose many of the band's hits, including "Bohemian Rhapsody",
sold for £1.7 million, while his handwritten lyrics for the song went for £1.38 million. The door of his Garden Lodge
home in west London, covered in graffiti left by fans, went for £412,750. The crown and cloak designed by Diana
Moseley for the 1986 Magic tour (his final concerts) sold for £635,000. A pair of black striped <color=#3366CC>Adidas</color> high-top shoes
(his principal stage footwear from 1984 onward) sold for £127,000. The final evening sale at Sotheby's on 6 September
took in £12.2 million ($15.4 million), while the six sales in total reached £39.9 million ($50.4 million), smashing
Sotheby's pre-auction estimates.

Japan
Japan is an island country in <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color>. Located in the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color> off the northeast coast of the <color=#3366CC>Asian mainland</color>, it is
bordered to the west by the <color=#3366CC>Sea of Japan</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Sea of Okhotsk</color> in the north, and the <color=#3366CC>East China Sea</color> in the south. The
<color=#3366CC>Japanese archipelago</color> consists of four major islands alongside over 14,000 smaller islands. Japan is divided into <color=#3366CC>47</color>
<color=#3366CC>administrative prefectures</color> and eight traditional regions, and around 75% of its terrain is mountainous and heavily
forested, concentrating its agriculture and highly urbanized population along its eastern <color=#3366CC>coastal plains</color>. With a
population of almost 123 million as of 2026, it is the world's 11th most populous country. <color=#3366CC>Tokyo</color> is the country's capital
and largest city.
The first known habitation of the <color=#3366CC>archipelago</color> dates to the <color=#3366CC>Upper Paleolithic</color>, with the beginning of the Japanese
Paleolithic dating to c. 36,000 BC. Between the 4th and 6th centuries, its kingdoms were united under an emperor in
<color=#3366CC>Nara</color> and later in <color=#3366CC>Heian-kyō</color>. From the 12th century, actual power was held by military aristocrats known as <color=#3366CC>shōgun</color> and
feudal lords called daimyō, enforced by warrior nobility named <color=#3366CC>samurai</color>. After rule by the Kamakura and <color=#3366CC>Ashikaga</color>
<color=#3366CC>shogunates</color> and <color=#3366CC>a century of warring states</color>, Japan was unified in 1600 by the <color=#3366CC>Tokugawa shogunate</color>, which
implemented <color=#3366CC>an isolationist foreign policy</color>. In 1853, <color=#3366CC>an American fleet</color> forced Japan to <color=#3366CC>open trade to the West</color>, which led
to the <color=#3366CC>end of the shogunate</color> and the <color=#3366CC>restoration of imperial power</color> in 1868.
The <color=#3366CC>Meiji period</color> saw Japan pursue rapid <color=#3366CC>industrialization</color>, <color=#3366CC>modernization</color>, militarism, and overseas colonization.
Declaring itself an <color=#3366CC>imperial power</color> in 1889 with the promulgation of the Meiji Constitution, it <color=#3366CC>annexed Taiwan</color> in 1895,

followed by <color=#3366CC>Korea</color> in 1910. In 1937, Japan <color=#3366CC>invaded China</color> and <color=#3366CC>attacked the U.S.</color> and <color=#3366CC>European colonial powers</color> in 1941,
thus entering World War II as an <color=#3366CC>Axis power</color>. After being defeated in the <color=#3366CC>Pacific War</color> and suffering the U.S. <color=#3366CC>atomic</color>
<color=#3366CC>bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki</color>, Japan <color=#3366CC>surrendered in 1945</color> and <color=#3366CC>came under Allied occupation</color> until 1952. It
underwent <color=#3366CC>rapid economic growth</color> in the following decades and became one of the first major non-NATO allies of the
U.S. Since the collapse of the Japanese asset price bubble in the early 1990s, it has experienced a prolonged period of
economic stagnation referred to as the <color=#3366CC>Lost Decades</color>.

Japan is a <color=#3366CC>constitutional monarchy</color> with a <color=#3366CC>bicameral</color> legislature known as the <color=#3366CC>National Diet</color>. Widely considered a <color=#3366CC>great</color>
<color=#3366CC>power</color> and the only Asian member of the <color=#3366CC>G7</color>, it maintains one of the world's strongest militaries but has constitutionally
renounced its right to declare war. A <color=#3366CC>developed country</color> with one of the world's largest economies by nominal GDP, it is
a global leader in the automotive, electronics, and robotics industries, in addition to making significant contributions to
science and technology. It has one of the world's highest life expectancies, but is undergoing a population decline. The

<color=#3366CC>culture of Japan</color> is well known around the world, particularly <color=#3366CC>its popular culture</color> as expressed in <color=#3366CC>animation</color>, <color=#3366CC>art</color>, <color=#3366CC>comics</color>,
<color=#3366CC>cuisine</color>, fashion, <color=#3366CC>films</color>, <color=#3366CC>music</color>, television, <color=#3366CC>theater</color>, and video games.
Etymology
The name for Japan in <color=#3366CC>Japanese</color> is written using the <color=#3366CC>kanji</color> and is pronounced Nihon or Nippon. Before was adopted in
the early 8th century, the country was known in China as Wa (changed in Japan around 757 to ) and in Japan by the
endonym Yamato. Nippon, the original Sino-Japanese reading of the characters, is favored for official uses, including
on Japanese banknotes and postage stamps. Nihon is typically used in everyday speech and reflects shifts in
Japanese phonology during the <color=#3366CC>Edo period</color>. The characters mean 'sun origin', which is the source of the popular
Western epithet "Land of the Rising Sun".
The name "Japan" is based on <color=#3366CC>Min</color> or <color=#3366CC>Wu Chinese</color> pronunciations of and was introduced to European languages
through early trade. In the 13th century, <color=#3366CC>Marco Polo</color> recorded the Early Mandarin Chinese pronunciation of the
characters as Cipangu. The old <color=#3366CC>Malay</color> name for Japan, Japang or Japun, was borrowed from a southern coastal
Chinese dialect and encountered by <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color> traders in <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>, who brought the word to Europe in the early
16th century. The first version of the name in English appears in a book published in 1577, which spelled the name as
Giapan in a translation of a 1565 Portuguese letter.
History
Prehistoric to classical history
Modern humans arrived in Japan around 38,000 years ago (~36,000 BC), marking the beginning of the Japanese

Paleolithic. Around 14,500 BC (the start of the <color=#3366CC>Jōmon period</color>), a <color=#3366CC>Mesolithic</color> to <color=#3366CC>Neolithic</color> semi-sedentary <color=#3366CC>hunter-gatherer</color>
culture characterized by pit dwelling and rudimentary agriculture emerged. Clay vessels from the period are among the
oldest surviving examples of pottery. The Japonic-speaking Yayoi people later entered the archipelago from the Korean
Peninsula, intermingling with the Jōmon people. The <color=#3366CC>Yayoi period</color> saw the introduction of innovative practices including
<color=#3366CC>wet-rice farming</color>, a new style of pottery, and metallurgy from China and Korea. According to legend, <color=#3366CC>Emperor Jimmu</color>
(descendant of <color=#3366CC>Amaterasu</color>) founded a kingdom in central Japan in 660 BC, beginning <color=#3366CC>a continuous imperial line</color>.
Japan first appears in written history in the Chinese <color=#3366CC>Book of Han</color>, completed in 111 AD, where it is described as having
a hundred small kingdoms. A century later, the Book of Wei records that the kingdom of Yamatai (which may refer to
Yamato) unified many of these kingdoms. <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color> was introduced to Japan from <color=#3366CC>Baekje</color> (a Korean kingdom) in 552,
but the development of Japanese Buddhism was primarily influenced by China. Despite early resistance, Buddhism
was promoted by the ruling class, including figures like <color=#3366CC>Prince Shōtoku</color>, and gained widespread acceptance beginning
in the <color=#3366CC>Asuka period</color> (592–710).
In 645, the government led by Prince Naka no Ōe and Fujiwara no Kamatari devised and implemented the far-reaching
<color=#3366CC>Taika Reforms</color>. The Reform began with land reform, based on Confucian ideas and <color=#3366CC>philosophies</color> from <color=#3366CC>China</color>. It
nationalized all land in Japan, to be distributed equally among cultivators, and ordered the compilation of a household
registry as the basis for a new system of taxation. The true aim of the reforms was to bring about greater centralization
and to enhance the power of the imperial court, which was also based on the governmental structure of China. Envoys
and students were dispatched to China to learn about Chinese writing, politics, art, and religion.
The Jinshin War of 672, a bloody conflict between Prince Ōama and his nephew Prince Ōtomo, became a major
catalyst for further administrative reforms. These reforms culminated with the promulgation of the Taihō Code, which
consolidated existing statutes and established the structure of the central and subordinate local governments. These
legal reforms created the ritsuryō state, a system of Chinese-style centralized government that remained in place for
half a millennium.
The Nara period (710–784) marked the emergence of a Japanese state centered on the Imperial Court in Heijō-kyō
(modern <color=#3366CC>Nara</color>). The period is characterized by the appearance of a nascent <color=#3366CC>literary culture</color> with the completion of the
<color=#3366CC>Kojiki</color> (712) and <color=#3366CC>Nihon Shoki</color> (720), as well as the development of Buddhist-inspired artwork and architecture. A
smallpox epidemic in 735–737 is believed to have killed as much as one-third of Japan's population. In 784, Emperor
Kanmu moved the capital, settling on <color=#3366CC>Heian-kyō</color> (modern-day <color=#3366CC>Kyoto</color>) in 794. This marked the beginning of the <color=#3366CC>Heian</color>
<color=#3366CC>period</color> (794–1185), during which a distinctly indigenous Japanese culture emerged. <color=#3366CC>Murasaki Shikibu</color>'s <color=#3366CC>The Tale of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Genji</color> and the lyrics of Japan's national anthem "<color=#3366CC>Kimigayo</color>" were written during this time.
Feudal era
Japan's feudal era was characterized by the emergence and dominance of a ruling class of warriors, the <color=#3366CC>samurai</color>. In
1185, following the defeat of the Taira clan by the Minamoto clan in the <color=#3366CC>Genpei War</color>, samurai <color=#3366CC>Minamoto no Yoritomo</color>
established a military government at Kamakura. After Yoritomo's death, the Hōjō clan came to power as regents for the
shōgun. The <color=#3366CC>Zen</color> school of Buddhism was introduced from China in the Kamakura period (1185–1333) and became
popular among the samurai class.
The <color=#3366CC>Kamakura shogunate</color> repelled <color=#3366CC>Mongol invasions</color> in 1274 and 1281 but <color=#3366CC>was eventually overthrown</color> by <color=#3366CC>Emperor</color>
<color=#3366CC>Go-Daigo</color>. Go-Daigo was defeated by <color=#3366CC>Ashikaga Takauji</color> in 1336, beginning the <color=#3366CC>Muromachi period</color> (1336–1573). The
succeeding Ashikaga shogunate failed to control the feudal warlords (daimyō) and a civil war began in 1467, opening
the century-long <color=#3366CC>Sengoku period</color> ('Warring States').
During the 16th century, Portuguese traders and <color=#3366CC>Jesuit</color> missionaries reached Japan, initiating direct commercial and
cultural exchange between Japan and the West. <color=#3366CC>Oda Nobunaga</color> used European technology and firearms to conquer
many other daimyō; his consolidation of power began the Azuchi–Momoyama period. After the death of Nobunaga in
1582, his successor, <color=#3366CC>Toyotomi Hideyoshi</color>, unified the nation in the early 1590s and launched <color=#3366CC>two unsuccessful</color>
<color=#3366CC>invasions of Korea in 1592 and 1597</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Tokugawa Ieyasu</color> served as regent for Hideyoshi's son Toyotomi Hideyori within the Council of Five Elders and used
his position to gain political and military support. When open war broke out, Ieyasu defeated rival clans in the <color=#3366CC>Battle of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Sekigahara</color> in 1600. He was appointed shōgun by Emperor Go-Yōzei in 1603 and established the <color=#3366CC>Tokugawa</color>
<color=#3366CC>shogunate</color> at Edo (modern Tokyo). The shogunate enacted measures including Buke shohatto, as a code of conduct to
control the autonomous daimyō, and in 1639 the isolationist <color=#3366CC>sakoku</color> ('closed country') policy that spanned the two and a
half centuries of tenuous political unity known as the <color=#3366CC>Edo period</color> (1603–1868). Modern Japan's economic growth began
in this period, resulting in roads (Kaidō) and water transportation routes, as well as financial instruments such as
<color=#3366CC>futures contracts</color>, banking and insurance of the Osaka rice brokers. The study of Western sciences (rangaku)
continued through contact with the Dutch enclave in <color=#3366CC>Nagasaki</color>. The Edo period gave rise to kokugaku ('national
studies'), the study of Japan by the Japanese.
Modern era
The United States Navy sent Commodore <color=#3366CC>Matthew C. Perry</color> to force the opening of Japan to the outside world. Arriving
at Uraga with four "Black Ships" in July 1853, the <color=#3366CC>Perry Expedition</color> resulted in the March 1854 Convention of
Kanagawa. Subsequent similar treaties with other Western countries brought economic and political crises. The
resignation of the shōgun led to the <color=#3366CC>Boshin War</color> and the establishment of a <color=#3366CC>centralized state</color> nominally unified under
the emperor (the <color=#3366CC>Meiji Restoration</color>). Adopting Western political, judicial, and military institutions, the Cabinet organized
the Privy Council, introduced the Meiji Constitution (November 29, 1890), and assembled the <color=#3366CC>Imperial Diet</color>.
During the <color=#3366CC>Meiji period</color> (1868–1912), the <color=#3366CC>Empire of Japan</color> emerged as the most developed state in <color=#3366CC>Asia</color> and as an
industrialized world power that pursued military conflict to expand its sphere of influence. After victories in the <color=#3366CC>First</color>
<color=#3366CC>Sino-Japanese War</color> (1894–1895) and the <color=#3366CC>Russo-Japanese War</color> (1904–1905), Japan gained control of Taiwan, Korea
and the southern half of <color=#3366CC>Sakhalin</color>, and annexed Korea in 1910. The Japanese population doubled from 35 million in
1873 to 70 million by 1935, with a significant shift to urbanization.
The early 20th century saw a period of Taishō democracy (1912–1926) overshadowed by increasing <color=#3366CC>expansionism</color> and
militarization. World War I allowed Japan, which joined the side of the victorious <color=#3366CC>Allies</color>, to capture <color=#3366CC>German possessions</color>
in the <color=#3366CC>Pacific</color> and China in <color=#3366CC>1920</color>. The 1920s saw a political shift towards statism, a period of lawlessness following the
1923 <color=#3366CC>Great Tokyo Earthquake</color>, the passing of laws against political dissent, and a series of attempted coups.
This process accelerated in the 1930s, spawning several radical nationalist groups that shared a hostility to liberal
democracy and a dedication to expansion in Asia. In 1931, Japan <color=#3366CC>invaded China and occupied Manchuria</color>, which led to
the establishment of <color=#3366CC>puppet state</color> of <color=#3366CC>Manchukuo</color> in 1932. Following international condemnation of the occupation,
Japan resigned from the <color=#3366CC>League of Nations</color> in 1933. In 1936, Japan signed the Anti-Comintern Pact with <color=#3366CC>Nazi</color>
<color=#3366CC>Germany</color>; the 1940 Tripartite Pact made it one of the <color=#3366CC>Axis powers</color>.
The Empire of Japan invaded other parts of China in 1937, precipitating the <color=#3366CC>Second Sino-Japanese War</color> (1937–1945).
In 1940, the Empire invaded French Indochina, after which the United States placed an oil embargo on Japan. On
December 7–8, 1941, Japanese forces carried out surprise <color=#3366CC>attacks on Pearl Harbor</color>, as well as on British forces in
<color=#3366CC>Malaya</color>, Singapore, and <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color>, among others, beginning <color=#3366CC>World War II in the Pacific</color>. Throughout areas occupied
by Japan during the war, <color=#3366CC>numerous abuses</color> were committed against local inhabitants. Many women were forced into
<color=#3366CC>sexual slavery</color>.
After <color=#3366CC>Allied</color> victories during the next four years, which culminated in the <color=#3366CC>Soviet invasion of Manchuria</color> and the <color=#3366CC>atomic</color>
<color=#3366CC>bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki</color> in 1945, Japan agreed to <color=#3366CC>an unconditional surrender</color>. The war cost Japan
millions of lives and many of its conquered territories, including de jure parts of Japan such as <color=#3366CC>Korea</color>, <color=#3366CC>Taiwan</color>, Karafuto,
and the <color=#3366CC>Kurils</color>. The Allies, led by the United States, repatriated millions of Japanese settlers from their former colonies
and military camps throughout Asia, largely eliminating the <color=#3366CC>Empire of Japan</color> and its influence over the territories it
conquered. The Allies convened the <color=#3366CC>International Military Tribunal for the Far East</color> to prosecute Japanese leaders,
notably excluding <color=#3366CC>Emperor Hirohito</color>, for <color=#3366CC>war crimes</color> and <color=#3366CC>crimes against humanity</color>.
In 1947, Japan adopted a new constitution emphasizing liberal democratic practices. The <color=#3366CC>Allied occupation</color> ended with
the <color=#3366CC>Treaty of San Francisco</color> in 1952, and Japan was granted membership in the <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color> in 1956. <color=#3366CC>A period of</color>
<color=#3366CC>record growth</color> propelled Japan to become the world's second-largest economy at that time; this ended in the mid-1990s
after the popping of an asset price bubble, beginning the "<color=#3366CC>Lost Decade</color>" characterized by economic stagnation and low
inflation. On March 11, 2011, Japan suffered the <color=#3366CC>Tōhoku earthquake</color>—the largest by magnitude in its recorded
history—which, along with the ensuing tsunami, triggered the <color=#3366CC>Fukushima nuclear accident</color>. On May 1, 2019, after the
historic abdication of Emperor Akihito, his son <color=#3366CC>Naruhito</color> became Emperor, beginning the Reiwa era.
Geography
Japan comprises 14,125 islands that extend along the Pacific coast of Asia. It stretches over 3000 km
northeast–southwest from the <color=#3366CC>Sea of Okhotsk</color> to the <color=#3366CC>East China Sea</color>. The country's five main islands, from north to

south, are <color=#3366CC>Hokkaido</color>, <color=#3366CC>Honshu</color>, <color=#3366CC>Shikoku</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kyushu</color> and <color=#3366CC>Okinawa</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Ryukyu Islands</color>, which include Okinawa, are a chain
to the south of Kyushu. The Nanpō Islands are south and east of the main islands of Japan. Together they are often
known as the <color=#3366CC>Japanese archipelago</color>. As of 2019, Japan's territory is 377,975.24 km². Japan has the sixth-longest
coastline in the world at 29751 km. Because of its far-flung outlying islands, Japan's exclusive economic zone is the
eighth-largest in the world, covering 4470000 km².
The Japanese archipelago is 67% forests and 14% agricultural. The primarily rugged and mountainous terrain is
restricted for habitation. Thus the habitable zones, mainly in the coastal areas, have very high population densities:
Japan is the 40th most densely populated country even without considering that local concentration. Honshu has the
highest population density at 450 persons/km2 (1200/sq mi) as of 2010, while Hokkaido has the lowest density of 64.5
persons/km2 as of 2016. As of 2014, approximately 0.5% of Japan's total area is <color=#3366CC>reclaimed land</color> (umetatechi). <color=#3366CC>Lake</color>
<color=#3366CC>Biwa</color> is an ancient lake and the country's largest freshwater lake.
Japan is substantially prone to earthquakes, <color=#3366CC>tsunami</color> and volcanic eruptions because of its location along the <color=#3366CC>Pacific</color>
<color=#3366CC>Ring of Fire</color>. It has the 17th highest natural disaster risk as measured in the 2016 World Risk Index. Japan has 111
active volcanoes. Destructive earthquakes, often resulting in tsunami, occur several times each century; the <color=#3366CC>1923</color>
<color=#3366CC>Tokyo earthquake</color> killed over 140,000 people. More recent major quakes are the 1995 <color=#3366CC>Great Hanshin earthquake</color> and
the <color=#3366CC>2011 Tōhoku earthquake</color>, which triggered a large tsunami.
Climate
The climate of Japan is predominantly temperate but varies greatly from north to south. The northernmost region,
Hokkaido, has a humid continental climate with long, cold winters and very warm to cool summers. <color=#3366CC>Precipitation</color> is not
heavy, but the islands usually develop deep snowbanks in the winter.
In the <color=#3366CC>Sea of Japan</color> region on Honshu's west coast, northwest winter winds bring heavy snowfall during winter. In the
summer, the region sometimes experiences extremely hot temperatures because of the <color=#3366CC>Foehn</color>. The Central Highland
has a typical inland humid continental climate, with large temperature differences between summer and winter. The
mountains of the <color=#3366CC>Chūgoku</color> and <color=#3366CC>Shikoku</color> regions shelter the <color=#3366CC>Seto Inland Sea</color> from seasonal winds, bringing mild weather
year-round.
The Pacific coast features a <color=#3366CC>humid subtropical climate</color> that experiences milder winters with occasional snowfall and hot,
humid summers because of the southeast seasonal wind. The Ryukyu and Nanpō Islands have a <color=#3366CC>subtropical climate</color>,
with warm winters and hot summers. Precipitation is very heavy, especially during the rainy season. The main rainy
season begins in early May in Okinawa, and the rain front gradually moves north. In late summer and early autumn,
<color=#3366CC>typhoons</color> often bring heavy rain. According to the Environment Ministry, heavy rainfall and increasing temperatures
have caused problems in the agricultural industry and elsewhere. The highest temperature ever measured in Japan,
41.8 °C, was recorded on August 5, 2025.
Biodiversity
Japan has nine forest ecoregions which reflect the climate and geography of the islands. They range from <color=#3366CC>subtropical</color>
<color=#3366CC>moist broadleaf forests</color> in the Ryūkyū and <color=#3366CC>Bonin Islands</color>, to <color=#3366CC>temperate broadleaf and mixed forests</color> in the mild climate
regions of the main islands, to <color=#3366CC>temperate coniferous forests</color> in the cold, winter portions of the northern islands. Japan
has over 90,000 species of wildlife as of 2019, including the <color=#3366CC>brown bear</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Japanese macaque</color>, the Japanese
raccoon dog, the small Japanese field mouse, and the <color=#3366CC>Japanese giant salamander</color>. There are 53 Ramsar wetland sites
in Japan. Five sites have been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List for their outstanding natural value.
Environment
In the period of rapid economic growth after World War II, environmental policies were downplayed by the government
and industrial corporations; as a result, environmental pollution was widespread in the 1950s and 1960s. Responding
to rising concerns, the government introduced environmental protection laws in 1970. The <color=#3366CC>oil crisis in 1973</color> also
encouraged the efficient use of energy because of Japan's lack of natural resources.
Japan ranks 20th in the 2018 Environmental Performance Index, which measures a country's commitment to
environmental sustainability. Japan is the world's fifth-largest emitter of <color=#3366CC>carbon dioxide</color>. As the host and signatory of the
1997 <color=#3366CC>Kyoto Protocol</color>, Japan is under treaty obligation to reduce its carbon dioxide emissions and to take other steps to
curb climate change. In 2020, the government of Japan announced a target of carbon-neutrality by 2050.
Environmental issues include urban air pollution (NOx, suspended <color=#3366CC>particulate matter</color>, and <color=#3366CC>toxics</color>), <color=#3366CC>waste management</color>,
water <color=#3366CC>eutrophication</color>, nature conservation, <color=#3366CC>climate change</color>, chemical management and international co-operation for
conservation.
Government and politics
Japan is a <color=#3366CC>unitary state</color> and <color=#3366CC>constitutional monarchy</color> in which the power of the emperor (Tennō) is limited to a
ceremonial role. Executive power is instead wielded by the prime minister and the Cabinet, whose sovereignty is
vested in the Japanese people. <color=#3366CC>Naruhito</color> is the Emperor of Japan, having succeeded his father <color=#3366CC>Akihito</color> upon his
accession to the Chrysanthemum Throne in 2019.
Japan's legislative organ is the <color=#3366CC>National Diet</color>, a <color=#3366CC>bicameral</color> parliament. It consists of a lower House of Representatives
with 465 seats, elected by popular vote every four years or when dissolved, and an upper Senate with 248 seats,
whose popularly elected members serve six-year terms. There is <color=#3366CC>universal suffrage</color> for adults over 18 years of age,
with a secret ballot for all elected offices. The prime minister as the <color=#3366CC>head of government</color> has the power to appoint and
dismiss Ministers of State, and is appointed by the emperor after being designated from among the members of the
Diet. Sanae Takaichi is Japan's prime minister; she took office after winning the 2025 Liberal Democratic Party
leadership election and securing a confidence and supply agreement with Ishin. The broadly conservative <color=#3366CC>Liberal</color>
<color=#3366CC>Democratic Party</color> has been the dominant party in the country since the 1950s, often called the 1955 System.
Historically influenced by <color=#3366CC>Chinese law</color>, the Japanese legal system developed independently during the Edo period
through texts such as Kujikata Osadamegaki. Since the late 19th century, the judicial system has been largely based
on the <color=#3366CC>civil law</color> of Europe, notably Germany. In 1896, Japan established a <color=#3366CC>civil code</color> based on the German Bürgerliches
Gesetzbuch, which remains in effect with post–World War II modifications. The Constitution of Japan, adopted in 1947,
is the oldest unamended constitution in the world. Statutory law originates in the legislature, and the constitution
requires that the emperor promulgate legislation passed by the Diet without giving him the power to oppose legislation.
The main body of Japanese statutory law is called the Six Codes. Japan's court system is divided into four basic tiers:
the Supreme Court and three levels of lower courts.
